Static and Dynamic Characteristics of Measuring Instruments: Definitions, Time Constant, Solved Example and Calibration Tests

Accuracy, hysteresis and drift tell you how good a reading is once the process settles. Time constant, lag and dynamic error tell you how far the reading trails behind when the process moves fast.

Static terms Time constant Solved example Calculator Calibration tests

Every instrument datasheet mixes steady state terms like accuracy and linearity with time based terms like response time. Below we separate the two groups, work out a first order step response and test both on a calibration bench.

Hello everyone, today we are going to learn the static and dynamic characteristics of measuring instruments, with a solved time constant example, a calculator and the calibration tests for each.
Quick Answer

What are static and dynamic characteristics of an instrument?

Static and dynamic characteristics describe how an instrument behaves with a steady input and with a changing input. Static terms include accuracy, precision, sensitivity, resolution, linearity, hysteresis, dead zone, drift, range and span. Dynamic terms include speed of response, lag, fidelity, dynamic error and time constant. For example, a first order sensor with τ = 8 s reaches 63.2% of a step change after 8 s and about 99.3% after 40 s.

What Are Static and Dynamic Characteristics of Instruments?

The static and dynamic characteristics of an instrument are the two sets of performance terms that tell you how well it measures. Static terms apply when the input is steady, and dynamic terms apply when the input is changing with time.

Key Facts
  • Static terms come from point by point calibration against a reference.
  • Dynamic terms come from a step, ramp or sine input watched over time.
  • A first order sensor reaches 63.2% of a step at one time constant, 95% at three and over 99.3% at five.

A transmitter that is accurate on the bench can still read late in a fast loop, so you need to check static and dynamic characteristics together. Read common calibration terms first if as found and as left are new to you.

Advertisement

What Are the Static Characteristics of Measuring Instruments?

Static characteristics describe the relation between input and output once the reading has fully settled. We check them at fixed points across the range, so time is not part of the test.

Accuracy

Closeness of the reading to the true value, as a percent of span or reading.

Best for: Datasheet comparison
Closeness
Precision

Agreement between repeated readings of the same input.

Best for: Repeatability checks
Spread
Sensitivity

Output change divided by input change, such as 1.6 mA per bar.

Best for: Gain and scaling
Slope
Resolution

Smallest input change that gives a visible output change.

Best for: Digital displays and ADC
Smallest step
Linearity

Largest deviation of the curve from a straight line, in percent of span.

Best for: Transmitter curves
Straightness
Hysteresis

Output difference at one input approached rising, then falling.

Best for: Bourdon gauges, valves
Up vs down
Dead zone

Largest input change that gives no output change, also called dead band.

Best for: Valves, switches, gears
No response
Drift

Slow output change at constant input, as zero drift or span drift.

Best for: Calibration intervals
Time shift
Range and span

Range is 0 to 10 bar for example; span is the difference, 10 bar.

Best for: Sizing and scaling
Limits

Accuracy and precision are often confused, so keep the target shooting picture of accuracy versus precision in mind. A gauge can repeat to 0.1% and still read 2% high; that gauge is precise but not accurate.

In digital systems the ADC bit count sets the resolution, the smallest step you can see. Our note on PLC analog input resolution shows how 12 bit and 16 bit cards differ.

Transmitter 0 to 10 bar, output 4 to 20 mA
Span = 10 minus 0 = 10 bar
Sensitivity = 16 mA ÷ 10 bar = 1.6 mA/bar
At 5 bar: rising 12.02 mA, falling 12.10 mA
Hysteresis = 0.08 ÷ 16 × 100 = 0.5% of span

You can repeat the error part with our calibration error calculator and compare it with the datasheet limit.

Do You Know?

The ISA automation dictionary notes that dead band is expressed as a percent of span and causes phase lag between input and output. So a static fault also hurts loop dynamics.

What Are the Dynamic Characteristics of an Instrument?

Dynamic characteristics describe how the output follows an input that changes with time. They tell you how fast the instrument responds and how much error it shows while the process is moving.

Speed of response
How quickly the instrument reacts to a change, often given as t0.9.
Measuring lag
Delay in response: a retardation lag that rises slowly, or a pure time delay.
Fidelity
How faithfully the output copies the shape of a changing input.
Dynamic error
True value minus reading at any instant while the input changes.
Time constant
For a first order sensor, the time taken to reach 63.2% of a step change in input.

Tutorialspoint lists speed of response, dynamic error, fidelity and lag as the four main dynamic terms. The time constant ties them together for a first order sensor such as a thermometer in a well.

In the field you will see these terms as response time on a temperature sensor datasheet and as damping on a smart transmitter. The damping setting of a pressure transmitter adds time constant on purpose to calm a noisy signal.

Quick Tip

When a loop looks sluggish, check transmitter damping before you retune the controller. Damping is a time constant you added yourself.

How Do You Calculate a First Order Step Response?

You calculate it with y(t) = y0 + (yf minus y0) × (1 minus 1/e^(t/τ)), where τ is the time constant. After one τ the reading has covered 63.2% of the change.

John Cimbala of Penn State shows in his dynamic system notes that the output reaches about 95% at three time constants and over 99.3% at five. So we treat a sensor as settled after five time constants.

Solved example: RTD in a thermowell, τ = 8 s
Step from 30 °C to 130 °C, find reading at t = 16 s
t/τ = 16 ÷ 8 = 2, so 1/e² = 0.1353
y = 30 + 100 × (1 minus 0.1353)
Reading = 116.47 °C (86.47% of step)
Dynamic error = 130 minus 116.47 = 13.53 °C
Time to 99% = 4.6 τ = 36.8 s

The curve below plots this example. The last few degrees take as long as the first sixty, which is typical of a first order lag.

First Order Sensor Reading After Time t
Reading after time t
Reading 116.47 (86.47% of the step), dynamic error 13.53

If you want a second check on response time, the sensor response time calculator on Zenta Calculator does the same first order maths. For the electrical side of the same exponential curve, see our RC and RL time constant guide.

What Is the Difference Between Static and Dynamic Characteristics?

The main difference is time: static terms are measured after the output settles, while dynamic terms are measured while it is still changing. A good instrument needs both a small static error and a response fast enough for the process.

PointStaticDynamic
Input typeConstant or very slowStep, ramp or sine
Main termsAccuracy, precision, linearity, hysteresisTime constant, lag, fidelity, dynamic error
Test method5 point calibration up and downStep test with a timer or recorder
Typical unit% of span or % of readingSeconds, t0.5, t0.63, t0.9
Fixed byZero and span trim, linearisationDamping, sensor design, thermowell choice
Matters most forCustody transfer, quality, recordsFast loops, trips, alarms
What a static calibration tells you
  • Error at each test point
  • Hysteresis and linearity
  • Zero and span drift
What it does not tell you
  • Settling time after a change
  • Lag from thermowell or impulse lines
  • Effect of damping on the loop
Myth: A more accurate instrument is always a faster one.
Fact: Accuracy is static and response time is dynamic; an accurate RTD in a thick thermowell can be very slow.
Myth: The time constant is the time to reach the final value.
Fact: One time constant gives only 63.2% of the change; you need about five time constants to get within 0.7%.
Myth: Raising damping makes the reading more accurate.
Fact: Damping only smooths noise; it adds lag and can hide a real fast change in the process.

How to Test Static and Dynamic Characteristics During Calibration

You test static and dynamic characteristics separately: static terms with a five point check rising and falling against a reference, and dynamic terms with a step input and a timer. You can do both on the same bench with a hand pump or a temperature bath.

1
Record as found
Note readings at 0, 50 and 100% before any adjustment.
2
Exercise the sensor
Run it over the full range three times first.
3
Go upscale
Apply 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% and record both readings.
4
Go downscale
Come back 100 to 0% without overshooting any point.
5
Work out the errors
Find error, linearity and hysteresis in percent of span.
6
Run the step test
Apply a sudden step and time the output to 63.2% for τ, or to 90% for t0.9.

The reference must be clearly better than the instrument under test, which is the idea behind the test uncertainty ratio of at least 4 to 1. For pressure, a dead weight tester or a good multifunction calibrator serves as the reference.

Do You Know?

WIKA explains that IEC 60751 response time tests move the sensor into water flowing at 0.3 m/s or air at 3 m/s, with a temperature step of 10 to 30 K. The results are given as t0.5, t0.63 and t0.9.

For temperature sensors, do the step test with the sensor in the actual thermowell if you can. The air gap between sheath and well bore is often the biggest part of the time constant, as our thermowell guide explains.

Quick Tip

Never pass a downscale point and come back up to it. That reversal hides part of the hysteresis loop.

Always write both as found and as left results on the calibration certificate. Labs accredited by NABL under ISO/IEC 17025 also add a measurement uncertainty to every result.

Why Does an Instrument Show Poor Static or Dynamic Performance?

Poor static performance usually comes from drift, wear, wrong ranging or a bad reference, while poor dynamic performance usually comes from added lag. The table lists the symptoms we see most in plants and the first thing to check.

SymptomLikely causeWhat to check
Same offset at every pointZero shiftZero trim, mounting position
Error grows with inputSpan error or driftSpan trim, sensor ageing
Rising and falling readings differHysteresis or frictionBourdon tube, linkage, valve packing
Output ignores small changesDead zoneGear backlash, positioner dead band
Reading trails the processLarge time constantThermowell gap, damping value

If every point is off by the same amount, look at zero and span errors before blaming the sensor. A control loop that hunts around set point can also point to dead band, as covered in control valve hunting.

  • Damping set to the value written in the loop design, not left at the factory default
  • Sensor spring loaded against the thermowell tip
  • Impulse lines free of trapped air or liquid
  • Reference standard within its calibration date

Static and Dynamic Characteristics FAQ

What is the difference between static and dynamic characteristics with example?

Static characteristics use a steady input, like 0.5% hysteresis on a 0 to 10 bar transmitter. Dynamic characteristics use a changing input, like an 8 s time constant for an RTD in a thermowell.

You need both static and dynamic characteristics to judge whether an instrument suits a process.

How to calculate the time constant of a sensor from a step test?

Apply a sudden step input and record the output against time; the time constant is the time to cover 63.2% of the change.

For a step from 30 to 130 °C, note when the reading passes 93.2 °C. If that happens 8 s after the step, τ is 8 s.

What is the reading of a first order sensor after two time constants?

After two time constants the reading has covered 86.5% of the step. For a step from 30 to 130 °C with τ of 8 s, the reading at 16 s is 116.47 °C, a dynamic error of 13.53 °C.

That gap keeps shrinking but never quite reaches zero.

Why is hysteresis not the same as dead zone in instruments?

Hysteresis is the output difference at one input approached rising and then falling. Dead zone is a band of input change that gives no output change at all.

Both come from friction and backlash, so valve diagnostics often report them as one combined number.

What is a common mistake when testing hysteresis during calibration?

The usual mistake is overshooting a downscale point and coming back up to it. That reversal puts the reading on the rising curve and hides part of the hysteresis, so approach every downscale point from above.

Exercise the instrument over its full range before you start.

Which characteristic matters more for a fast control loop?

For a fast loop such as compressor surge control, dynamic terms matter more because lag delays every correction. Static accuracy still matters, since a fast but drifting transmitter controls tightly to the wrong value.

A small time constant and low damping are the first things to check.

What We Learn Today

  • Static and dynamic characteristics split instrument performance into steady state terms like accuracy and hysteresis and time based terms like lag and time constant.
  • A first order sensor covers 63.2% of a step in one time constant, 86.5% in two, 95% in three and over 99.3% in five.
  • Static terms are tested with a five point rising and falling calibration, while dynamic terms are tested with a step input and a timer.
